title: Do You Need a Degree to Be a Software Developer?
dek: No, you do not strictly need a degree to be a software developer — many work without one — but a degree still lowers friction with some employers. What actually gets you hired is demonstrable skill and a portfolio.

seo.metaTitle: Do You Need a Degree to Be a Developer?
seo.metaDescription: Do you need a degree to be a software developer? An honest look at when a degree helps, when it doesn't, and what actually gets you hired instead.

sources.label: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Software Developers, Quality Assurance Analysts, and Testers, Occupational Outlook Handbook

body.richText: This is one of the most-asked questions in tech, and the honest answer is nuanced: no, a degree is not strictly required, but it is not useless either. Let us separate what is true from what people wish were true — in both directions.

The honest verdict: you can absolutely become a software developer without a degree, and many people have. A degree is a helpful shortcut through certain hiring filters, not a mandatory ticket. Skills and a portfolio decide most outcomes.

The BLS lists a bachelor's degree as the typical entry-level education for software developers — "typical" meaning common, not required. The same field reported a median annual wage of $133,080 in May 2024 and projects 15% growth from 2024 to 2034, much faster than average. It is a strong field whether or not you take the degree route.

items: Passing strict HR filters at large, traditional companies
Qualifying for certain visa and immigration pathways that require a degree
Roles in specialized fields (e.g., some systems, security, or research work)
Giving you a structured foundation in computer science fundamentals

body.text: When you do not need one

items: Many startups and mid-size tech companies hire on demonstrated skill
Web and application development roles are especially portfolio-driven
Contract and freelance work is judged almost entirely on what you can build
Self-taught and bootcamp graduates work throughout the industry

body.richText: The no-degree path is not the easy path. Without a degree you must be more disciplined and more visible: a stronger portfolio, real projects, and often more persistence in the job hunt. "No degree required" does not mean "no work required."

richText: Degree or not, the hiring signal is the same: can you build working software and explain how you did it? That means real projects, a public portfolio, and the ability to pass a technical interview. Start by learning a language well — see

items.question: Can you be a software developer without a degree?
items.answerRichText: Yes. Many working developers are self-taught or came through bootcamps. Employers that hire this way judge you on demonstrable skill and a portfolio rather than a diploma.

items.question: Is it harder to get a developer job without a degree?
items.answerRichText: It can be, at companies with strict filters. You offset that with a stronger portfolio, real projects, and persistence. In portfolio-driven roles, the gap narrows significantly.

items.question: What should I learn to become a developer without a degree?
